verdict.reasoning: Patient says: 'recently I'm wheezy. Uh, I have feel like kind of short of breath' and when asked duration: 'Mmm, two, three days. Yeah, quite recently.'
Patient: 'I have cough and cough a lot, and I have a fever' and later confirms temperature: 'Uh, thirty seven, yeah.' No sputum: 'Have you coughed any phlegm up...?' 'No.' This supports a dry cough.

Patient describes dyspnea on exertion: 'I also used to walk to work but recently I can't because... I feel like very short of breath' and difficulty finishing sentences: 'sometimes I feel like I can't even finish sentence is quite difficult to... complete the talking sometimes.'

When asked if short of breath at rest: 'at the moment, are you... feeling short of breath when you're sitting still? Or just when you walk?' Patient: 'Just walk... currently I feel, I feel well.' Also: 'Have you been woken up at night time at all?' Patient: 'No.'

Patient: 'I also used to walk to work but recently I can't' and later: 'at the moment... Just walk or sometimes, but currently I feel, I feel well.' Ability to climb stairs: 'Are you able to get up and down the stairs OK?' Patient: 'Yeah.'

Childhood asthma: 'Uh, yes, I had asthma.' Severity and hospital: 'when you were a child how bad was your asthma?' Patient: 'Uh, it's quite bad.' and 'did you ever have to go to hospital with it?' Patient: 'Yeah, sometimes.' No ICU: 'Did you ever get severely unwell, have to be on intensive care unit...?' Patient: 'No, not that bad.'
Patient: 'I also had, uh, hay fever and eczema' and later: 'Any other medical problems?' Patient: 'Uh, I have, uh, hay fever as well.'
Patient: 'I also had, uh, hay fever and eczema.'

Salbutamol inhaler: 'Um, I took salbutamol? Salbutamol? Yeah.' Frequency and use: 'OK, so you, you normally take that do you?' Patient: 'Normally, yeah.' and 'how often do you normally need it?' Patient: 'Every, every few weeks?...' and 'What about when you exercise normally, do you have to use medication? Uh, inhalers?' Patient: 'Yeah.'
Doctor: 'and do you take any other medications?' Patient: 'No, nothing else.'
Doctor: 'And any allergies to medications?' Patient: 'No, no allergies.'

Smoking: 'Do you smoke?' Patient: 'No, I don't smoke.' Alcohol: 'Do you drink any alcohol regularly?' Patient: 'Yeah, one glass.' ... 'Every two or three days? Depends, yeah.' and specifies: 'one glass of wine.'
Living situation: 'Who do you live with, do you live on your own, or do you live with' Patient: 'I live with my partner.' Job: 'what's your job, day-to-day?' Patient: 'Uh, I'm engineer.'
Work status: 'have you been at work in the last few days?' Patient: 'No I can't because I used to walk walk to work, but recently I, I work from home or sometimes I take sick leave, yeah.'

Duration and symptoms: see cc-001 and hpi-001/002. Doctor: 'it sounds like you've had a flare up of your asthma.' Possible triggers: 'It could be, um, triggered by, if there's more pollen around, or... you may have a viral infection, causing it to get worse.' This summarizes an asthma exacerbation with wheeze, dyspnea on exertion, dry cough, and possible allergy/viral trigger.
Allergic rhinitis corresponds to hay fever. Patient: 'I also had, uh, hay fever' and later: 'I have, uh, hay fever as well.'

Doctor: 'what I would suggest is you take it more regularly... if you increase it so you're taking it two to four puffs, like, every four hours? Initially.' This refers to the asthma inhaler (Salbutamol).

Doctor: 'Have you got, um, a spacer at home?' Patient: 'No.' Doctor: 'what I can do is, I can prescribe you... a spacer to use your inhaler a bit more efficiently, which the pharmacist can show you how you use that when you pick it up.'

Doctor: 'I can prescribe you a peak flow meter so we can check your breathing level' and later: 'when you get the peak flow meter... if you can record a value first thing when you wake up... And in the evening over the next week.'

Doctor: 'if you get a high temperature or your wheezing is getting worse, you need to call us back straightaway so we can just advise you further with that.' This is safety-net advice regarding fever and worsening wheeze/shortness of breath.

Doctor: 'it will be a good idea when you're feeling better if we can arrange just a review... You could arrange a review in a week or so' and 'then we can discuss [peak flow] over the phone... and see whether you need to go on another inhaler as well.' This implies controller inhaler consideration based on PEF and symptoms.

Doctor: 'the other thing to do would be to take a regular antihistamine. Which you can get from the pharmacy, I can put a on your notes about what to take.' This is a regular OTC antihistamine for allergic symptoms with pharmacist involvement.
